text: Syed Ali Shah Geelani (29 September 1929 – 1 September 2021) was a pro-Pakistan Islamist separatist leader active in the Islamic insurgency in the Indian union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, regarded as the father of Jihadi Separatism in the region.[13][14][15][19][20][21] Born in 1929 in Zurimanz, Aloosa tehsil, Bandipora district of North Kashmir, into a Syed family, he was the son of a landless labourer in the canals department. He received part of his education in Sopore and the rest in Lahore, studying at a madrasa attached to Masjid Wazir Khan and later enrolling in Oriental College, where he completed the Adib 'Alim course in Islamic theology.[23][21][11] After returning to Kashmir, he joined the Jammu & Kashmir National Conference, serving as secretary of its unit in Zurimanj and working as a reporter for Akhbar-i-Khidmat under Maulana Sayeed Masoodi. Masoodi sponsored his further studies in Urdu, Persian, and English, after which he became a school teacher in Pathar Masjid and later at Rainawari in Srinagar, where he encountered Saaduddin Tarabali, a follower of Maulana Abul A'la Maududi. Maududi’s hardline Islamist ideology, which emphasized Islam as the foundation of political order, deeply influenced Geelani, who later stated that Maududi had "beautifully.. expressed the feelings that lay deep down in my own heart".[24] He became a full-fledged member of Jamaat-e-Islami in 1952 and taught its literature to students while addressing mosque congregations. He contested the 1971 Indian general election as an independent candidate but lost to Syed Ahmed Aga, with Jamaat alleging ballot-rigging. He won the Sopore seat in the 1972 and 1977 legislative assembly elections on a Jamaat-e-Islami ticket, but lost in 1983 due to sympathy for the National Conference following the death of Sheikh Abdullah. He also contested the 1977 general election as an independent candidate, losing to Abdul Ahad Vakil. In the 1987 assembly election, Geelani won under the Muslim United Front (MUF) coalition but was expelled from it in 1988 and resigned as MLA in August 1989 due to allegations of ballot rigging. He was viewed as a key separatist leader, with Omar Abdullah blaming him for militancy and Farooq Abdullah urging him to prevent further destruction. A founding member of the All Parties Hurriyat Conference (APHC) in 1993, he was initially chosen as its chairman but Mirwaiz Umar Farooq was selected instead due to secular majority in the alliance. He became chairman in 1998 and was replaced by Abdul Ghani Bhat on 20 July 2000. In 2003, the Jamaat-e-Islami removed him from the Hurriyat executive and later from the head of its political bureau, appointing Ashraf Sehrai. The appointment of Mohammad Abbas Ansari as Hurriyat chairman caused a split in September 2003, leading Geelani to form the All Parties Hurriyat Conference (G), which he led for three years, replacing interim chairman Masarat Alam Bhat. He was re-elected in 2006 despite wanting to step down due to ill health and appointed lifetime chairman in 2015. In February 2004, he sought to form his own party, which was prohibited by Jamaat-e-Islami, leading to his suspension; he later dropped the idea and attempted to take over the organization’s leadership, and was readmitted in August 2004, after which he founded the Tehreek-e-Hurriyat and was elected chairman for three years in October 2004. He was re-elected in 2007, 2010, and 2013, and received a one-year extension in 2017 due to election disruptions during the 2016–2017 unrest. Jamaat-e-Islami removed him from its advisory council in 2005, distanced itself from him, and stated he represented only Tehreek-e-Hurriyat. In April 2010, he was temporarily expelled for defending the freedom of the author of his biography Qaid-e-Inqilab – Ek Tareekh, Ek Tehreek, but was later restored as a basic member. Geelani called for numerous general strikes in response to deaths of militants and civilians in Kashmir. He urged a complete boycott of the 2014 legislative assembly elections, rejecting proposals for self-rule or autonomy from the People's Democratic Party and National Conference, though record voter turnout of over 65% was achieved, leading to criticism from Indian media for misleading the public. He was invited to participate in the OIC and Kashmir Contact Group meeting in New York in September 2015 and sent a letter to the UN after Burhan Muzaffar Wani’s killing, listing six confidence-building measures. In March 2018, he resigned as chairman of Tehreek-e-Hurriyat citing ill health, replaced by Ashraf Sehrai, but remained chairman of his faction of the APHC. In June 2020, he resigned from the faction, accusing it of nepotism and corruption and misinterpreting his speeches, though the faction refused to accept the resignation and did not appoint a new chairman until after his death. On 29 November 2010, Geelani, along with Arundhati Roy, Varavara Rao, and others, was charged under sections 124A (sedition), 153A (promoting enmity), 153B (imputations prejudicial to national integration), 504 (insult intended to provoke breach of peace), and 505 (false statement with intent to cause mutiny or offence), read with Section 13 of the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, 1967, due to a seminar titled "Azadi-the Only Way" in New Delhi where he was heckled. He lived in Hyderpora, Srinagar, and had two sons—Nayeem and Naseem—and four daughters—Anisha, Farhat Jabeen, Zamshida, and Chamshida. Anisha and Farhat are from his second marriage. Nayeem and his wife, both doctors, lived in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, before returning to India in 2010; Naseem works as a Senior scientist at Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology in Srinagar. His grandson Izhaar is a crew member in a private airline in India; Farhat is a madani teacher in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, with a husband who is an engineer there; other grandchildren study in leading Indian schools. His cousin Ghulam Nabi Fai is in London. Ruwa Shah, daughter of Altaf Ahmad Shah (SAS Geelani’s son-in-law), is a journalist who previously worked with Al Jazeera, IANS, and The Indian Express. Geelani’s passport was seized in 1981 over "anti-India" activities; except for his 2006 Hajj pilgrimage, he was not allowed to leave India. In 2007, his condition worsened, and he was advised surgery abroad, but his visa request to the U.S. was rejected due to his violent approach in the Kashmir conflict, leading him to go to Mumbai for surgery; supporters and family claimed this was a "human rights violation". On 6 March 2014, he fell ill with a severe chest infection after returning to Srinagar and has been under house arrest since 2010, with renewed house arrest upon return. In May 2015, he applied for a passport to visit his daughter in Saudi Arabia, which was withheld on technical grounds, including failure to fill the nationality column; a nine-month passport was granted on humanitarian grounds after he acknowledged Indian nationality. Rumors of his death in March 2014, spread through false edits to his Wikipedia article and Facebook pages by a Hindi news channel, led to internet and phone service suspensions in Kashmir, though the then Chief Minister Omar Abdullah attributed the cuts to a power line and optical fiber failure due to snowfall. After the 2019 Pulwama attack, India took stronger action against pro-Pakistan separatists, including Geelani, with the Enforcement Directorate levying a penalty of ₹14.40 lakh and confiscating nearly ₹6.8 lakh in foreign exchange under the Foreign Exchange Management Act. Geelani reportedly developed breathing complications and died on 1 September 2021 at his Hyderpora residence in Srinagar due to prolonged illness. His son Naseem alleged that police raided the house, took the body forcibly, and buried it in a graveyard in Hyderpora during the night, with no close family members allowed to attend, though they visited the next morning. Director General Dilbag Singh denied the allegations. Restrictions on travel and internet were imposed in Kashmir after his death. On 2 September 2021, an FIR was registered against his family under the UAPA for clothing his body with a Pakistani flag and raising "anti-national" slogans. Kashmiri political leaders and members of the Government of Pakistan condoled his death, with Prime Minister Imran Khan ordering flags to be flown at half-mast. On 14 August 2020, Pakistani President Arif Alvi conferred the Nishan-e-Pakistan on Geelani for his decades-long struggle for Kashmiris’ right to self-determination. In February 2014, he criticized custodial violence in Indian jails, citing the denial of a meeting to parents of Javaid Ahmad Khan, calling it "state terrorism". He is viewed as sympathetic to Jamaat-e-Islami, and his official residence was considered Jamaat property before being donated to the Milli Trust. In November 2011, he called for protests against what he described as "objectionable anti-Islamic" content on Facebook, which led to minor clashes with security forces. Geelani condemned the U.S. killing of Osama bin Laden and stated he would lead last rite prayers in absentia for bin Laden in Srinagar, though a European Union delegation canceled a scheduled meeting with him. He supported Afzal Guru, accused in the 2001 Indian Parliament attack, and Hafiz Saeed, a mastermind of the 2008 Mumbai attacks and Lashkar-e-Taiba chief. Geelani maintained that while Pakistan supported the indigenous struggle of Kashmiris, it did not mean Pakistan could take decisions on their behalf. He supported a dialogue process aimed at resolving the Kashmir issue in accordance with the people’s wishes and aspirations.

The Kashmir Valley experienced minor clashes between protestors and security forces. Geelani condemned the U.S. killing of Osama bin Laden and stated he would lead last rite prayers in absentia in Srinagar for the slain al-Qaeda leader after Bin Laden's death in May 2011. Following large-scale prayers for Osama in a congregation of thousands of Kashmiris, a European Union delegation cancelled a scheduled meeting with him. He supported Afzal Guru, accused in the 2001 Indian Parliament attack, and Hafiz Saeed, a mastermind of the 2008 Mumbai Attacks and chief of Lashkar-e-Taiba. Geelani asserted that while Pakistan supports the "indigenous struggle" of the people of Jammu and Kashmir morally, diplomatically, and politically, this does not mean Pakistan can decide on their behalf. He advocated for a dialogue process on the Kashmir issue that reflects the wishes and aspirations of the Kashmiri people, but believed such dialogue between India and Pakistan begins under diplomatic compulsions and is merely a time-delaying tactic. He maintained that Kashmiris are not enemies of India and do not hold grudges against its inhabitants, emphasizing that a strong India and Pakistan are possible only if the Kashmir issue is resolved for regional peace, prosperity, and development. He stated that Kashmir is not a border dispute between India and Pakistan that can be resolved through bilateral understandings, but rather an issue concerning the future of 15 million people, and that without the involvement of Kashmiri people, dialogue has been meaningless in the past and will remain so. He called for India to immediately and unconditionally release political prisoners and withdraw pending court cases against youth that have been ongoing for 20 years. Geelani has been repeatedly criticised by Indian authorities for inciting violence in the Kashmir Valley and for working as an offshoot of Pakistan. He openly stated that he was not Indian, explaining that travelling on an Indian passport is a necessity for every Kashmiri due to the region's international status as a disputed area between India and Pakistan. He declared, "We are Pakistani; Pakistan is ours," in a gathering of his supporters. While Geelani personally believed Kashmir should merge with Pakistan, he was known for standing up to both Indian and Pakistani governments, refusing to engage with anyone, including former Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf, who did not support the right to self-determination for Kashmir. Sheikh Mustafa Kamal, a senior leader of the Jammu & Kashmir National Conference and son of Sheikh Abdullah, criticised Geelani for acting on "dictations" from Pakistan and accused him of being a "double agent" on the payroll of Pakistan's ISI. Pakistan openly supported Geelani; a three-member delegation from the Pakistan High Commission, led by Abdul Basit, met him at his Malviya Nagar residence in March 2015. Abdul Basit assured Geelani of full support, stating Pakistan's position on Kashmir remains unchanged despite regime changes in New Delhi. He also invited Geelani to attend the Pakistan Day function on 23 March. The Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi routinely invites pro-separatist leaders from Jammu and Kashmir. On 14 August, the Pakistani government awarded him its highest civilian honour, the Nishan-e-Pakistan. Over the decades, Geelani consistently refused proposals from both the Indian and Pakistani governments and remained committed to the United Nations-promised plebiscite of 1948.
